chapter: With Chick Webb and Ella Fitzgerald, 1936-39
title: Jack Robbins's music-publishing deal
summary: Publisher Jack Robbins offered free arrangements and early hit songs for a weekly coast-to-coast Savoy broadcast.

story.theme_name: Radio and television work: staff jobs, shows and broadcasts
story.community_name: Working radio and television: network shows, studio staffs, talk-show bands

blocks.x: And I had made a trip down to visit my friend, Jack Robbins. And he had talked to me about a deal where he would support us in the arrangement.
See, he's a -- got -- hired Greggman to come in to help him with the big three companies. A lot of pictures were coming out of Hollywood and had all these hit songs.
He asked me if I would -- if we would broadcast from the Savoy once a week, coast to coast. And that was a very important broadcast.
That was going straight across the to California board (Inaudible) -- so many states (Inaudible), you know.
So he gave me a song and I got -- Edgar Sampson at that time was with the (Inaudible). band.
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943
And Edgar Sampson made the arrangements on it and it came out pretty good.
And we broadcasted that Saturday afternoon. It was a Robbins song. So anyway, Jack told me -- he say, "Look" --
Jack Robbins.
Jack Robbins. I say -- Jack told me, he say, "Come down Monday, I want to talk to you," after he heard the broadcast.
What was the song, by the way?
I forget what the name of it now. Just one of those songs that came out with one of the pictures.

At that time, they had a lot of things. It was like song pluggers. They were plugging -- Like, everybody had a song picture come out (Paramount [inaudible]), United Artists, all the different pictures they had. Show times (inaudible), the big productions, things like that.
So Jack say, "Yall have the best thing in
S. & S. REPORTING COMPANY, INC. WOrth 2-2915 WOrth 2-2943
the country. I'll give you a deal. We'll take care all the arrangements, and all you got to do is just broadcast."

"We're going to give you a lot of arrangements. We're going to give you the hit songs that come out before anybody get the hit songs, because we feel that Ella Fitzgerald is about a top thing right now."
"We think she's really going to be tops." He's looking way ahead of what I'm thinking about.
I'm just thinking, "Well, here's a guy that's going to give us some music," you know.

Another thing I told Chick Webb, "Look, Jack want to give us a deal. He wants to -- he's going to give us all the top songs. And whatever the arrangements cost, you know, they'll dissolve it themselves."
Because they have song pluggers running all around the country, you know, plugging songs, and this will be the way so that they can get plugged.
And Jack had a couple of bands (inaudible) at

that time. He had a band at the Pennsylvania Hotel. They were playing all the Jack Robbins songs. He say, "Okay." So he began to give us all these top songs. And we began to move Ella Fitzgerald out of that other class of singing. We'd move her into the pop.
